--- PAGE 1 ---
Lab Report – Prallel and distributed computing lab




Name: Abdul Samad, Roll number: 243203624  Input size: 20000  Algorithm: bubble sort

Recorded program output
serial.c roll number = 243203624 input size
= 20000 serial execution time =
1.039000034332 seconds first value = 1
last value = 32767

attempt.c roll number = 243203624 input
size = 20000 attempt execution time =
0.246999979019 seconds first value = 3
last value = 32767 sorted correctly = no

parallel.c roll number = 243203624 input
size = 20000 parallel execution time =
0.095999956131 seconds first value = 1
last value = 32767 threads = 12

Output comparison
serial out.txt: 20000 values
parallel out.txt: 20000 values
Compare-Object result: Outputs identical.
Therefore, the corrected parallel sequence is identical to the serial sequence.

Parallelization and correction
The serial program performs bubble sort with one thread. The first attempt places an OpenMP parallel-for over dependent bubble-sort passes.
Threads can update overlapping array elements at the same time, creating a race condition; the recorded result confirms this with sorted correctly
= no.

The corrected parallel program divides the input into four disjoint ranges. OpenMP sections sort the ranges concurrently, so each thread owns
separate data and no critical section or lock is needed for swaps. After the sections complete, the ranges are merged serially. This removes the
race condition while preserving the selected sorting algorithm.

Speedup and interpretation
Speedup = serial time / parallel time
Speedup = 1.039000034332 / 0.095999956131 = 10.823

The corrected version is faster because independent ranges are sorted concurrently. The attempt is faster than serial in this run but is invalid
because its result is incorrect. The recorded machine team had 12 OpenMP threads. Ubuntu lscpu and nproc could not be recorded in this Windows
environment because WSL is not installed; available host equivalents were CPU(s) = 12, Core(s) per socket = 6, Thread(s) per core = 2, and nproc
equivalent = 12.

Further optimization
A further optimization would parallelize the merge stage as well. It could reduce the remaining serial work, but thread scheduling, memory
bandwidth, synchronization, and the small size of individual merge tasks could eliminate the expected benefit on the machine used.

--- ARCHIVE MEMBER: attempt.c ---
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 20000

static void firstParallelAttempt(int values[], int size)
{
#pragma omp parallel for
    for (int pass = 0; pass < size - 1; pass++)
    {
        for (int index = 0; index < size - pass - 1; index++)
        {
            if (values[index] > values[index + 1])
            {
                int temporary = values[index];
                values[index] = values[index + 1];
                values[index + 1] = temporary;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2)
    {
        printf("Usage: %s <roll_number>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int rollNumber = atoi(argv[1]);
    int values[ARRAY_SIZE];
    srand((unsigned int)rollNumber);

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        values[index] = rand();
    }

    double start = omp_get_wtime();
    firstParallelAttempt(values, ARRAY_SIZE);
    double end = omp_get_wtime();

    printf("roll number = %d\n", rollNumber);
    printf("input size = %d\n", ARRAY_SIZE);
    printf("attempt\n");
    printf("execution time = %.12f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("first value = %d\n", values[0]);
    printf("last value = %d\n", values[ARRAY_SIZE - 1]);

    int sorted = 1;
    for (int index = 1; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        if (values[index - 1] > values[index])
        {
            sorted = 0;
            break;
        }
    }
    printf("sorted correctly = %s\n", sorted ? "yes" : "no");
    return 0;
}

--- ARCHIVE MEMBER: parallel.c ---
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 20000
#define SECTION_COUNT 4

static void bubbleSortRange(int values[], int left, int right)
{
    for (int pass = left; pass < right - 1; pass++)
    {
        int swapped = 0;

        for (int index = left; index < right - (pass - left) - 1; index++)
        {
            if (values[index] > values[index + 1])
            {
                int temporary = values[index];
                values[index] = values[index + 1];
                values[index + 1] = temporary;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }

        if (!swapped)
        {
            break;
        }
    }
}

static void mergeRanges(int values[], int temporary[], int left, int middle, int right)
{
    int leftIndex = left;
    int rightIndex = middle;
    int outputIndex = left;

    while (leftIndex < middle && rightIndex < right)
    {
        if (values[leftIndex] <= values[rightIndex])
        {
            temporary[outputIndex++] = values[leftIndex++];
        }
        else
        {
            temporary[outputIndex++] = values[rightIndex++];
        }
    }

    while (leftIndex < middle)
    {
        temporary[outputIndex++] = values[leftIndex++];
    }

    while (rightIndex < right)
    {
        temporary[outputIndex++] = values[rightIndex++];
    }

    for (int index = left; index < right; index++)
    {
        values[index] = temporary[index];
    }
}

static void parallelBubbleSort(int values[], int size, int *threadCount)
{
    int temporary[ARRAY_SIZE];
    int firstEnd = size / SECTION_COUNT;
    int secondEnd = firstEnd * 2;
    int thirdEnd = firstEnd * 3;

#pragma omp parallel shared(values, threadCount)
    {
#pragma omp single
        *threadCount = omp_get_num_threads();

#pragma omp sections
        {
#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, 0, firstEnd);

#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, firstEnd, secondEnd);

#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, secondEnd, thirdEnd);

#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, thirdEnd, size);
        }
    }

    mergeRanges(values, temporary, 0, firstEnd, secondEnd);
    mergeRanges(values, temporary, secondEnd, thirdEnd, size);
    mergeRanges(values, temporary, 0, secondEnd, size);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2)
    {
        printf("Usage: %s <roll_number>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int rollNumber = atoi(argv[1]);
    int values[ARRAY_SIZE];
    int threadCount = 0;
    srand((unsigned int)rollNumber);

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        values[index] = rand();
    }

    double start = omp_get_wtime();
    parallelBubbleSort(values, ARRAY_SIZE, &threadCount);
    double end = omp_get_wtime();

    FILE *output = fopen("parallel out.txt", "w");
    if (output == NULL)
    {
        printf("Could not create parallel out.txt\n");
        return 1;
    }

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        fprintf(output, "%d\n", values[index]);
    }
    fclose(output);

    printf("roll number = %d\n", rollNumber);
    printf("input size = %d\n", ARRAY_SIZE);
    printf("parallel\n");
    printf("execution time = %.12f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("first value = %d\n", values[0]);
    printf("last value = %d\n", values[ARRAY_SIZE - 1]);
    printf("threads = %d\n", threadCount);
    return 0;
}

--- ARCHIVE MEMBER: serial.c ---
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 20000

static void bubbleSort(int values[], int size)
{
    for (int pass = 0; pass < size - 1; pass++)
    {
        int swapped = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < size - pass - 1; index++)
        {
            if (values[index] > values[index + 1])
            {
                int temporary = values[index];
                values[index] = values[index + 1];
                values[index + 1] = temporary;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }

        if (!swapped)
        {
            break;
        }
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2)
    {
        printf("Usage: %s <roll_number>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int rollNumber = atoi(argv[1]);
    int values[ARRAY_SIZE];
    srand((unsigned int)rollNumber);

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        values[index] = rand();
    }

    double start = omp_get_wtime();
    bubbleSort(values, ARRAY_SIZE);
    double end = omp_get_wtime();

    FILE *output = fopen("serial out.txt", "w");
    if (output == NULL)
    {
        printf("Could not create serial out.txt\n");
        return 1;
    }

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        fprintf(output, "%d\n", values[index]);
    }
    fclose(output);

    printf("roll number = %d\n", rollNumber);
    printf("input size = %d\n", ARRAY_SIZE);
    printf("serial\n");
    printf("execution time = %.12f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("first value = %d\n", values[0]);
    printf("last value = %d\n", values[ARRAY_SIZE - 1]);
    return 0;
}


--- ARCHIVE MEMBER: Abdul Samad BSSE group A - 5th semester.pdf ---
--- PAGE 1 ---
Lab Report – Prallel and distributed computing lab




Name: Abdul Samad, Roll number: 243203624  Input size: 20000  Algorithm: bubble sort

Recorded program output
serial.c roll number = 243203624 input size
= 20000 serial execution time =
1.039000034332 seconds first value = 1
last value = 32767

attempt.c roll number = 243203624 input
size = 20000 attempt execution time =
0.246999979019 seconds first value = 3
last value = 32767 sorted correctly = no

parallel.c roll number = 243203624 input
size = 20000 parallel execution time =
0.095999956131 seconds first value = 1
last value = 32767 threads = 12

Output comparison
serial out.txt: 20000 values
parallel out.txt: 20000 values
Compare-Object result: Outputs identical.
Therefore, the corrected parallel sequence is identical to the serial sequence.

Parallelization and correction
The serial program performs bubble sort with one thread. The first attempt places an OpenMP parallel-for over dependent bubble-sort passes.
Threads can update overlapping array elements at the same time, creating a race condition; the recorded result confirms this with sorted correctly
= no.

The corrected parallel program divides the input into four disjoint ranges. OpenMP sections sort the ranges concurrently, so each thread owns
separate data and no critical section or lock is needed for swaps. After the sections complete, the ranges are merged serially. This removes the
race condition while preserving the selected sorting algorithm.

Speedup and interpretation
Speedup = serial time / parallel time
Speedup = 1.039000034332 / 0.095999956131 = 10.823

The corrected version is faster because independent ranges are sorted concurrently. The attempt is faster than serial in this run but is invalid
because its result is incorrect. The recorded machine team had 12 OpenMP threads. Ubuntu lscpu and nproc could not be recorded in this Windows
environment because WSL is not installed; available host equivalents were CPU(s) = 12, Core(s) per socket = 6, Thread(s) per core = 2, and nproc
equivalent = 12.

Further optimization
A further optimization would parallelize the merge stage as well. It could reduce the remaining serial work, but thread scheduling, memory
bandwidth, synchronization, and the small size of individual merge tasks could eliminate the expected benefit on the machine used.

IMSciences                                                      SWE 537


                   Institute of Management Sciences
                                      Peshawar
                    Assignment
                                   Parallel sorting

            SWE 537 — Parallel and Distributed Computing (Lab)

                           Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan
              BS Artificial Intelligence, BS Software Engineering   Fall 2026



Task

On the Ubuntu virtual machine, select one sorting algorithm. Measure the serial execution time. Con-
struct a parallel version. Measure the parallel execution time. Account for the results from the recorded
measurements.
  No parallel program is supplied. The written account must follow from the recorded execution.

1 Programs

Prepare three C source files.

1. serial.c performs the sort as a serial portion only. It contains no parallel construct.

2. attempt.c retains the first parallel version in the state in which the sorted result was incorrect, or the
   execution time exceeded the serial execution time. Do not modify this file after that execution.

3. parallel.c is the corrected version. Its sorted output must be identical to that of serial.c.

    All three programs must compile and run on the Ubuntu virtual machine.
  When an execution time is under 0.2 seconds, increase the input size and repeat all three executions.
Use the same input size in all three.
   The input depends on the roll number, so that one submission cannot be substituted for another. Use
the roll number as the random seed. Generate the same unsorted data in each program.
   Each program reports, in this order:

• the roll number

• the input size

• serial, attempt, or parallel

• one execution time in seconds, taken by a wall-clock timer around the sort only

• the first value and the last value of the sorted sequence

   parallel.c also reports the number of threads that took part in the parallel region. This is the team
size during that region, not the value reported by nproc.
   serial.c writes the complete sorted sequence to serial out.txt. parallel.c writes the complete
sorted sequence to parallel out.txt. Each file contains the full sequence, one value after another, with
nothing omitted. The command diff serial out.txt parallel out.txt produces no output when the
sequences match.

2 Report (one page)

Each numerical value in the report must appear in the recorded output.

1. Include the lscpu fields CPU(s), Core(s) per socket, and Thread(s) per core, together with the output
   of nproc.

2. Include the recorded output of all three programs, and the result of diff serial out.txt parallel out.txt.

3. Identify the parallelized portion of the algorithm and the serial portion.


                                             1

--- PAGE 2 ---
IMSciences                                                      SWE 537



4. Compute the speedup from the serial execution time and the parallel.c execution time. Show the
   division.

5. The speedup need not equal nproc. Using the recorded execution times and the recorded processor
   information, account for the speedup obtained.

6. For attempt.c, state the defect in the result or in the execution time, and state the correction made
   in parallel.c.

7. State one further optimization that was not implemented. State the expected effect on execution time,
   and state what could invalidate that expectation on the machine used.

3 Submit

Submit one zip archive containing serial.c, attempt.c, parallel.c, and the one-page report.
  A complete submission is one in which the three programs compile, every reported value appears in
the recorded output, and diff serial out.txt parallel out.txt produces no output.





                                             2

==========================================================================================
FILE 4/36: Assignment 1\attempt.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 1608 bytes
==========================================================================================
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 20000

static void firstParallelAttempt(int values[], int size)
{
#pragma omp parallel for
    for (int pass = 0; pass < size - 1; pass++)
    {
        for (int index = 0; index < size - pass - 1; index++)
        {
            if (values[index] > values[index + 1])
            {
                int temporary = values[index];
                values[index] = values[index + 1];
                values[index + 1] = temporary;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2)
    {
        printf("Usage: %s <roll_number>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int rollNumber = atoi(argv[1]);
    int values[ARRAY_SIZE];
    srand((unsigned int)rollNumber);

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        values[index] = rand();
    }

    double start = omp_get_wtime();
    firstParallelAttempt(values, ARRAY_SIZE);
    double end = omp_get_wtime();

    printf("roll number = %d\n", rollNumber);
    printf("input size = %d\n", ARRAY_SIZE);
    printf("attempt\n");
    printf("execution time = %.12f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("first value = %d\n", values[0]);
    printf("last value = %d\n", values[ARRAY_SIZE - 1]);

    int sorted = 1;
    for (int index = 1; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        if (values[index - 1] > values[index])
        {
            sorted = 0;
            break;
        }
    }
    printf("sorted correctly = %s\n", sorted ? "yes" : "no");
    return 0;
}

==========================================================================================
FILE 6/36: Assignment 1\parallel.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 3590 bytes
==========================================================================================
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 20000
#define SECTION_COUNT 4

static void bubbleSortRange(int values[], int left, int right)
{
    for (int pass = left; pass < right - 1; pass++)
    {
        int swapped = 0;

        for (int index = left; index < right - (pass - left) - 1; index++)
        {
            if (values[index] > values[index + 1])
            {
                int temporary = values[index];
                values[index] = values[index + 1];
                values[index + 1] = temporary;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }

        if (!swapped)
        {
            break;
        }
    }
}

static void mergeRanges(int values[], int temporary[], int left, int middle, int right)
{
    int leftIndex = left;
    int rightIndex = middle;
    int outputIndex = left;

    while (leftIndex < middle && rightIndex < right)
    {
        if (values[leftIndex] <= values[rightIndex])
        {
            temporary[outputIndex++] = values[leftIndex++];
        }
        else
        {
            temporary[outputIndex++] = values[rightIndex++];
        }
    }

    while (leftIndex < middle)
    {
          temporary[outputIndex++] = values[leftIndex++];
    }

    while (rightIndex < right)
    {
        temporary[outputIndex++] = values[rightIndex++];
    }

    for (int index = left; index < right; index++)
    {
        values[index] = temporary[index];
    }
}

static void parallelBubbleSort(int values[], int size, int *threadCount)
{
    int temporary[ARRAY_SIZE];
    int firstEnd = size / SECTION_COUNT;
    int secondEnd = firstEnd * 2;
    int thirdEnd = firstEnd * 3;

#pragma omp parallel shared(values, threadCount)
    {
#pragma omp single
        *threadCount = omp_get_num_threads();

#pragma omp sections
        {
#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, 0, firstEnd);

#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, firstEnd, secondEnd);

#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, secondEnd, thirdEnd);

#pragma omp section
            bubbleSortRange(values, thirdEnd, size);
        }
    }

    mergeRanges(values, temporary, 0, firstEnd, secondEnd);
    mergeRanges(values, temporary, secondEnd, thirdEnd, size);
    mergeRanges(values, temporary, 0, secondEnd, size);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2)
    {
        printf("Usage: %s <roll_number>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int rollNumber = atoi(argv[1]);
    int values[ARRAY_SIZE];
    int threadCount = 0;
    srand((unsigned int)rollNumber);

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        values[index] = rand();
    }

    double start = omp_get_wtime();
    parallelBubbleSort(values, ARRAY_SIZE, &threadCount);
    double end = omp_get_wtime();

    FILE *output = fopen("parallel out.txt", "w");
    if (output == NULL)
    {
        printf("Could not create parallel out.txt\n");
        return 1;
    }

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        fprintf(output, "%d\n", values[index]);
    }
    fclose(output);

    printf("roll number = %d\n", rollNumber);
    printf("input size = %d\n", ARRAY_SIZE);
    printf("parallel\n");
    printf("execution time = %.12f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("first value = %d\n", values[0]);
    printf("last value = %d\n", values[ARRAY_SIZE - 1]);
    printf("threads = %d\n", threadCount);
    return 0;
}

SWE 537 - Parallel Sorting Report
Roll number: 243203624  Input size: 20000  Algorithm: bubble sort

Recorded program output
serial.c
roll number = 243203624
input size = 20000
serial
execution time = 1.039000034332 seconds
first value = 1
last value = 32767

attempt.c
roll number = 243203624
input size = 20000
attempt
execution time = 0.246999979019 seconds
first value = 3
last value = 32767
sorted correctly = no

parallel.c
roll number = 243203624
input size = 20000
parallel
execution time = 0.095999956131 seconds
first value = 1
last value = 32767
threads = 12
Output comparison
serial out.txt: 20000 values
parallel out.txt: 20000 values
Compare-Object result: Outputs identical.
Therefore, the corrected parallel sequence is identical to the serial sequence.
Parallelization and correction
The serial program performs bubble sort with one thread. The first attempt places an OpenMP parallel-for over dependent bubble-sort passes.
Threads can update overlapping array elements at the same time, creating a race condition; the recorded result confirms this with sorted
correctly = no.

The corrected parallel program divides the input into four disjoint ranges. OpenMP sections sort the ranges concurrently, so each thread owns
separate data and no critical section or lock is needed for swaps. After the sections complete, the ranges are merged serially. This removes the
race condition while preserving the selected sorting algorithm.
Speedup and interpretation
Speedup = serial time / parallel time
Speedup = 1.039000034332 / 0.095999956131 = 10.823

The corrected version is faster because independent ranges are sorted concurrently. The attempt is faster than serial in this run but is invalid
because its result is incorrect. The recorded machine team had 12 OpenMP threads. Ubuntu lscpu and nproc could not be recorded in this
Windows environment because WSL is not installed; available host equivalents were CPU(s) = 12, Core(s) per socket = 6, Thread(s) per core =
2, and nproc equivalent = 12.
Further optimization
A further optimization would parallelize the merge stage as well.  It could reduce the remaining serial work, but thread scheduling, memory
bandwidth, synchronization, and the small size of individual merge tasks could eliminate the expected benefit on the machine used.

==========================================================================================
FILE 9/36: Assignment 1\serial.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 1721 bytes
==========================================================================================
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define ARRAY_SIZE 20000

static void bubbleSort(int values[], int size)
{
    for (int pass = 0; pass < size - 1; pass++)
    {
        int swapped = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < size - pass - 1; index++)
        {
            if (values[index] > values[index + 1])
            {
                int temporary = values[index];
                values[index] = values[index + 1];
                values[index + 1] = temporary;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }

        if (!swapped)
        {
            break;
        }
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2)
    {
        printf("Usage: %s <roll_number>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int rollNumber = atoi(argv[1]);
    int values[ARRAY_SIZE];
    srand((unsigned int)rollNumber);

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        values[index] = rand();
    }

    double start = omp_get_wtime();
    bubbleSort(values, ARRAY_SIZE);
    double end = omp_get_wtime();

    FILE *output = fopen("serial out.txt", "w");
    if (output == NULL)
    {
        printf("Could not create serial out.txt\n");
        return 1;
    }

    for (int index = 0; index < ARRAY_SIZE; index++)
    {
        fprintf(output, "%d\n", values[index]);
    }
    fclose(output);

    printf("roll number = %d\n", rollNumber);
    printf("input size = %d\n", ARRAY_SIZE);
    printf("serial\n");
    printf("execution time = %.12f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("first value = %d\n", values[0]);
    printf("last value = %d\n", values[ARRAY_SIZE - 1]);
    return 0;
}


==========================================================================================
FILE 10/36: Lab Week 2\SE-A-Abdul_Samad\timeCalc.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 364 bytes
==========================================================================================
#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>
#define N 10000000000

int main(void)
{
    long i;
    long sum = 0;
    clock_t start, end;
    start = clock();
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        sum += i;
    }
    end = clock();

    printf("Sum = %d\n", sum);
    printf("Serial time = %f seconds\n", (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
}

==========================================================================================
FILE 12/36: Lab Week 2\SE-A-Abdul_Samad\timeCalc2.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 493 bytes
==========================================================================================
#include <stdio.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define N 1000000000LL

int main(void)
{
    long long i;
    long long sum = 0;
    double start, end;

    start = omp_get_wtime();
#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+ : sum)
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        sum += i;
    }
    end = omp_get_wtime();

    printf("Threads used = %d\n", omp_get_max_threads());
    printf("Sum = %lld\n", sum);
    printf("Parallel time = %.6f seconds\n", end - start);

    return 0;
}

#include <stdio.h>
#include <omp.h>

int main(void)
{
    omp_set_num_threads(4);

#pragma omp parallel
    {
#pragma omp sections
        {
#pragma omp section
            {
                printf("Task A thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num());
            }
#pragma omp section
            {
                printf("Task B thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num());
            }
#pragma omp section
            {
                printf("Task C thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num());
            }
#pragma omp section
            {
                printf("Task D thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num());
            }
        }
    }
}

FILE 17/36: Lab Week 3\task.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 443 bytes

#include <stdio.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define N 100000

int main(void)
{

    long i;
    long sum = 0;
// #pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum)
#pragma omp parallel
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        sum += i;
    }
    printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
}

// we got the race condition and we have shared storage and multiple processes are accessing
// it at the same it to avoid this race cnoidtion we use reduction

FILE 19/36: Lab Week 4\task.c
TYPE: .c
SIZE: 929 bytes

#include <stdio.h>
#include <omp.h>

#define N 500

int main(void)
{
    static double A[N][N];
    static double B[N][N];
    static double C[N][N];
    int i, j, k;
    double start, end;

    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
        {
            A[i][j] = 1.0;
            B[i][j] = 1.0;
            C[i][j] = 0.0;
        }
    }

    start = omp_get_wtime();
#pragma omp parallel for private(j,k)
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
        {
            double sum = 0.0;
// #pragma omp parallel for reduction(+ : sum)
            for (k = 0; k < N; k++)
            {
                sum += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
            }
            C[i][j] = sum;
        }
    }
    end = omp_get_wtime();
    printf("C[0][0] = %f (expected %d)\n", C[0][0], N);
    printf("serial time = %f seconds\n", end - start);
    return 0;
}

import socket 

server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
server.bind(("192.168.170.128", 12345))
server.listen(1)
print("Server listening on port 12345")

conn, addr = server.accept()
print("Connection from", addr)
data = conn.recv(1024).decode()
print("Recieved: ", data)
conn.send("Hello from Server!".encode())
conn.close()
server.close()

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void)
{

    int fd[2];
    pid_t pid;
    char message[] = "Hello from parent";
    char buffer[100];

    pipe(fd);
    pid = fork();
    if (pid > 0)
    {
        close(fd[0]);
        write(fd[1], message, strlen(message) + 1);
        close(fd(1));
    }
    else
    {
        close(fd[1]);
        read(fd[0], buffer, sizeof(buffer));
        printf("Child received: %s \n", buffer);
        close(fd[0]);
    }
}

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                  IMSciences
                             Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                           Week 1, Lab 1
                        Hardware: Program, Process, Thread, Core



1 Ideas

 • Program — the file on disk (hello.c, a.out). It is not running yet.

 • Process — one running copy of a program. Own memory. Two terminals running the same file =
  two processes.

 • Thread — a worker inside a process. Threads of one process share that memory. • Core

— hardware that runs a thread. More cores means more workers at the same time.

 • Socket  / hyperthreading  / cache — socket = one CPU chip (a laptop  is usually 1). Hyper
   threading: one core can show as 2 logical processors in lscpu (Thread(s) per core). Cache: small
   fast memory on the chip (L1 closest, then L2, L3 often shared).

       A program becomes a process. A process can have many threads. Threads run
                                    on cores.



2 Commands

Terminal

  lscpu
  free -h
  nproc



   nproc is how many logical processors Linux will give you. Same idea as CPU(s) in lscpu.
Write these lines from your lscpu:

 • CPU(s)

 • Socket(s)

 • Core(s) per socket

 • Thread(s) per core

 • L1d / L1i / L2 / L3

3 Reading lscpu

Example output

  CPU(s): 8
  Thread(s) per core: 2
  Core(s) per socket: 4
  Socket(s): 1

--- PAGE 2 ---
1 × 4 × 2 = 8 logical processors

   Four real cores, hyperthreading on, one chip. Parallel code can use more than one of these at
once. If nproc is 1, a parallel loop cannot show speedup on that machine.
4 A process from a program

C

  # include < stdio .h >

   int main ( void ) {
         printf ( " Hello from a process \ n " ) ;
        return 0;
   }



Terminal

  nano hello.c
  gcc hello.c -o hello
   ./hello

   This starts one process with one thread (the main thread).

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 1, Lab 2
                             Flynn’s Taxonomy and POSIX Threads




1 Ideas

Four ways a machine can issue instructions and touch data:

• SISD — Single Instruction, Single Data. Classic sequential CPU.

• SIMD — Single Instruction, Multiple Data. One instruction, many data (GPU, vector units).

• MISD — Multiple Instruction, Single Data. Rare.

• MIMD — Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data. Many cores, each can run a different instruction
  on different data. A typical lab PC or VM is MIMD.

   SPMD is not a Flynn class. Flynn describes the machine. SPMD is how the code is
         written: same C file, many threads or processes. MPI programs are often SPMD on
                         MIMD hardware.


2 Pthreads

A process starts with one main thread. pthread create starts extra workers in the same process.
They share memory.

• pthread create — start a thread.

• pthread join — wait until that thread finishes.  If main returns first, the process dies and the
   other threads stop.

• Compile with -pthread. Without it, the linker cannot find pthread create.

   Print order is not 1 then 2 then 3 then 4 every time. The OS scheduler picks who runs. Run the
program three times. If the order changes, that is the scheduler, not a broken printf.


3 Commands

Terminal

 nano hello_threads.c
 gcc -pthread hello_threads.c -o hello_threads
 ./hello_threads
 ./hello_threads
 ./hello_threads

nano: Ctrl+O, Enter (save), Ctrl+X (quit).
Forgot -pthread →undefined reference to pthread create.
Forgot ./ →command not found.

--- PAGE 2 ---
4 Program

Four threads. Each gets its own id in an array. Do not pass &i from the loop — that is one variable
four threads share.
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <pthread.h>

 void *hello(void *arg) {
     int id = *(int *)arg;
     printf("Hello from thread %d\n", id);
     return NULL;
 }

 int main(void) {
     pthread_t t[4];
     int id [4];
     int i;

     for (i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
         id[i] = i + 1;
         pthread_create (&t[i], NULL , hello , &id[i]);
      }

     for (i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
         pthread_join(t[i], NULL);
      }

     printf("main done\n");
     return 0;
 }

   Change 4 to 8 in both arrays and both loops, compile again, run. Eight Hellos, then main done.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 2, Lab 1
                                     Amdahl’s Law




1 Ideas

                                                                     Tserial
                                    speedup =
                                                                   Tparallel

  How many times faster than one worker.  If serial took 8 seconds and parallel took 2 seconds,
speedup = 4. That is not the same as “saved 6 seconds”.


2 Worked example

A program takes 20 seconds on one core.

• Loop (can run in parallel): 16 s

• Other work (stays serial: start, print, files): 4 s

   With N = 1 worker on the loop: still 16 + 4 = 20 s. Speedup = 1. Extra cores on the machine do
not help if the program still uses one.
   With N = 4 workers on the loop:

                                         16
                            T = 4 +  = 4 + 4 = 8 s
                                         4

                                             20
                                   speedup =  = 2.5
                                              8
   Not 4×. The 4 s of other work did not shrink.
     If the loop became instant (N →∞), the wait is still 4 s. Best possible speedup:

                                         20
                            = 5
                                          4

                 The serial remainder is a floor. Time cannot go below it.


3 Amdahl’s law

P = fraction of time that can run in parallel. 1 −P stays serial. N = workers.

                                              1
                              S =
                                       P
                                              (1 −P) +
                               N
   Same example: P = 16/20 = 0.8, so 1 −P = 0.2, N = 4:

                                 1             1         1
                   S =        =       =   = 2.5
                                0.20 + 0.80/4   0.20 + 0.20   0.40

   The parentheses are required. Without them the value is wrong.

--- PAGE 2 ---
4 Time view (same numbers)

                                                                        Tparallel part
                                           Tparallel = Tserial part +
                                 N

                                               16
                                       8 = 4 +
                                               4
   The formula and the time view must give the same result.


5 Numbers for this example

N = 4, total 20 s, loop 16 s, other 4 s:

• P = 0.8

• Tparallel = 8 s

• speedup = 2.5

• floor (loop →0) = 4 s, max speedup = 5

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 2, Lab 2
                             Serial and Parallel Programming with OpenMP




1 Ideas

• Serial — one worker (one core running the loop).

• Parallel — more than one worker at the same time, on the same machine.

• OpenMP — hints in C (#pragma omp ...), a small library, and -fopenmp. gcc creates threads.
  One computer, shared memory. Not MPI.

• pthread create starts threads by hand. OpenMP starts them for a for loop with one hint.

• Race — sum += i is look, add, write. Two threads can both see 7 and both write 8. Total is usually
   too small. Reduction — reduction(+:sum): private copies, then gcc adds them. Coherence is
   hardware, not this bug. Critical / lock is not used in these programs.

    speedup = Tserial/Tparallel. Serial 8 s and parallel 2 s ⇒speedup = 4, not “saved 6 seconds”.


2 Compile flag -fopenmp

The serial program has no #pragma, so it still runs on one thread. It still needs -fopenmp because it
uses omp get wtime() (wall-clock: how long you waited).
   clock() is not used here. clock() can add CPU time from every core, so four cores working 1
second can look like 4 seconds.
   omp get max threads() is how many OpenMP is allowed to hire. It can print 8 even in the serial
program. The serial loop still uses one thread because there is no #pragma. -fopenmp links the timer;
it does not turn a normal for into a team.


3 Commands

Terminal

 nproc
 nano serial.c
 gcc -fopenmp serial.c -o serial
 ./serial

 nano parallel.c
 gcc -fopenmp parallel.c -o parallel
 ./parallel
 export OMP_NUM_THREADS=2
 ./parallel
 export OMP_NUM_THREADS=4
 ./parallel

nproc should be 2 or more, or parallel will not get faster.
nano: Ctrl+O, Enter (save), Ctrl+X (quit).
Forgot ./ →command not found.
Forgot -fopenmp →error on omp.h, or still one thread.

--- PAGE 2 ---
4 Serial program (one worker)

C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 100000000

 int main(void) {
     long i;
     long sum = 0;
     double start , end;

     start = omp_get_wtime ();
     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          sum += i;
      }
     end = omp_get_wtime ();

     printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
     printf("serial time = %f seconds\n", end - start);
     return 0;
 }

     If the time is under 0.2 seconds, add a zero to N in both programs.


5 Parallel program (same loop)

The only new line:
C

 #pragma omp parallel for reduction (+: sum)

C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 100000000

 int main(void) {
     long i;
     long sum = 0;
     double start , end;

     start = omp_get_wtime ();
     #pragma omp parallel for reduction (+: sum)
     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          sum += i;
      }
     end = omp_get_wtime ();

     printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
     printf("parallel time = %f seconds\n", end - start);
     printf("threads = %d\n", omp_get_max_threads ());
     return 0;
 }

   The printed sum must match serial. If it does not, reduction is missing.

--- PAGE 3 ---
serial time
                              speedup =
                                                  parallel time

Four threads is not always 4× (Amdahl). Use the times from this run.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 3, Lab 1
                      OpenMP: Threads, Race, and Reduction




1 Ideas

• OpenMP — hints in C (#pragma omp ...), a small library, and -fopenmp. One process, shared
  memory. Not MPI. pthread create starts threads by hand; OpenMP: gcc starts them.

• #pragma omp parallel — every thread runs that block. Same source text is not the same work
   unless each thread uses different data or a worksharing construct. Four identical hellos only prove
   the team exists.

• #pragma omp parallel for — gcc splits one for loop. The word for on the pragma splits i.
  parallel alone around a sum loop means every thread runs the whole loop.

• omp set num threads(4) — team size. It overrides export OMP NUM THREADS when both are set.
  omp get thread num() — who am I. omp get num threads() — how many in the team right now
   (1 outside a parallel block). omp get max threads() — cap, even in a serial program.

• Race — sum += i is read, add, write. Total is usually too small. Reduction — private copies,
  then gcc adds them. Coherence is hardware, not this bug.

     main before / main after print once. Hello prints once per thread. Wrong sum = race.
                             Matching expected = reduction.


2 Commands

Terminal

 nano hello_openmp.c
 gcc -fopenmp hello_openmp.c -o hello
 ./hello

 nano race.c
 gcc -fopenmp race.c -o race
 ./race

 nano reduction.c
 gcc -fopenmp reduction.c -o reduction
 ./reduction

nano: Ctrl+O, Enter (save), Ctrl+X (quit).
Forgot ./ →command not found.
Forgot -fopenmp →error on omp.h, or still one thread.


3 Hello (the team)

C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

--- PAGE 2 ---
int main(void) {
     printf("main before\n");
     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     #pragma omp parallel
      {
         printf("hello from thread %d of %d\n",
                omp_get_thread_num (),
                omp_get_num_threads ());
      }

     printf("main after\n");
     return 0;
 }

   main before and main after print once. Hello prints once per thread (four times). The order of
the four hellos can change (OS scheduler).


4 Race (wrong total)

Expected for i = 0 to N-1:

                            N(N −1)
                                            2
   For N = 100000, expected = 4999950000.
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 100000

 int main(void) {
     long i;
     long sum = 0;

     #pragma omp parallel for
     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          sum += i;
      }

     printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
     printf("expected = %ld\n", (long)N * (N - 1) / 2);
     return 0;
 }

   Run three times. sum is usually not the expected value.


5 Reduction (correct total)

The only new clause:
C

 #pragma omp parallel for reduction (+: sum)

C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>



                                            2

--- PAGE 3 ---
#define N 100000

int main(void) {
    long i;
    long sum = 0;

    #pragma omp parallel for reduction (+: sum)
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
         sum += i;
     }

    printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
    printf("expected = %ld\n", (long)N * (N - 1) / 2);
    return 0;
}

  The printed sum must equal expected on every run.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 3, Lab 2
                      OpenMP: Sections, Single, and Critical




1 Ideas

• #pragma omp parallel — every thread runs that block.

• #pragma omp parallel for — gcc splits one for loop.

• sections — different named tasks, not slices of the same loop. Each section runs once. Order and
   thread ids can change.

• single — one thread runs that block. The others wait at the end of it, then all continue.

• critical — one thread at a time inside that { }. Reduction — private copies, then add (better
   for a sum). Critical — one key to the room (any shared update; a sum is slower).

    Each section runs once. Extra threads wait. Two threads and four sections: some threads
                                 do two jobs in a row.


2 Commands

Terminal

 nano omp_sections.c
 gcc -fopenmp omp_sections.c -o sections
 ./sections

 nano omp_single.c
 gcc -fopenmp omp_single.c -o single
 ./single

 nano omp_critical.c
 gcc -fopenmp omp_critical.c -o critical
 ./critical

nano: Ctrl+O, Enter (save), Ctrl+X (quit).
Forgot ./ →command not found.
Forgot -fopenmp →error on omp.h, or still one thread.


3 Sections (named tasks)

Four tasks. Four threads. Each of A, B, C, D prints once.
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 int main(void) {
     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     #pragma omp parallel
      {

--- PAGE 2 ---
#pragma omp sections
          {
             #pragma omp section
               {
                 printf("task A thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
               }
             #pragma omp section
               {
                 printf("task B thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
               }
             #pragma omp section
               {
                 printf("task C thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
               }
             #pragma omp section
               {
                 printf("task D thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
               }
          }
      }

     return 0;
 }

   Run three times. Write which thread id did A, B, C, and D each time. Extra threads with no
section left wait; they do not reprint A–D.


4 Single (one thread, then all continue)

main before and main after print once. single work prints once. after single prints once per
thread.
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 int main(void) {
     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     printf("main before\n");

     #pragma omp parallel
      {
         #pragma omp single
          {
             printf("single work thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
          }

         printf("after single thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
      }

     printf("main after\n");
     return 0;
 }

     If single work prints four times, the single directive is missing.


5 Critical (safe shared update)

Expected total for N = 100000:


                                            2

--- PAGE 3 ---
N(N −1)
                            = 4999950000
                                     2
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 100000

 int main(void) {
     long i;
     long sum = 0;

     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     #pragma omp parallel for
     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
         #pragma omp critical
          {
              sum += i;
          }
      }

     printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
     printf("expected = %ld\n", (long)N * (N - 1) / 2);
     return 0;
 }

   Run twice. Printed sum must equal expected both times. This is usually slower than reduction:
threads take turns on sum.

FILE 31/36: Lectures\Week-4-Lab-1.pdf
TYPE: .pdf
SIZE: 119511 bytes

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 4, Lab 1
                       OpenMP: Barrier, Atomic, and Locks




1 Ideas

• barrier — every thread stops at that line until all threads have arrived, then all continue. An
  after line comes only after every before line.

• atomic — one simple update is exclusive (example: sum += i). Same idea as critical, but for
  one statement, usually cheaper. Not a whole block of code.

• omp lock t — a lock you create: init, set (take), unset (give back), destroy. critical was a
   lock with no name.

• reduction is still the right tool for a fat sum. Atomic / critical / lock protect a shared update.

                             barrier = all threads wait, then all continue.
                                atomic = one add at a time.
                            lock = take the lock, update, then release it.


2 Commands

Terminal

 nano omp_barrier.c
 gcc -fopenmp omp_barrier.c -o barrier
 ./barrier

 nano omp_atomic.c
 gcc -fopenmp omp_atomic.c -o atomic
 ./atomic

 nano omp_lock.c
 gcc -fopenmp omp_lock.c -o lock
 ./lock

nano: Ctrl+O, Enter (save), Ctrl+X (quit).
Forgot ./ →command not found.
Forgot -fopenmp →error on omp.h, or still one thread.


3 Barrier

Four before lines, then four after lines. Thread ids can shuffle inside each group.
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 int main(void) {
     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     #pragma omp parallel

--- PAGE 2 ---
{
         printf("before barrier thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());

         #pragma omp barrier

         printf("after barrier thread %d\n", omp_get_thread_num ());
      }

     return 0;
 }

     If an after prints before all four before lines, the barrier is missing.


4 Atomic

Same expected total as the critical program, N = 100000:

                        N(N −1)
                            = 4999950000
                                     2
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 100000

 int main(void) {
     long i;
     long sum = 0;

     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     #pragma omp parallel for
     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
         #pragma omp atomic
          sum += i;
      }

     printf("sum = %ld\n", sum);
     printf("expected = %ld\n", (long)N * (N - 1) / 2);
     return 0;
 }

   Run twice. Printed sum must equal expected both times.


5 Lock

Loop i = 0 to 4. Expected 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 int main(void) {
     int i;
     int shared_var = 0;
     omp_lock_t lock;

     omp_set_num_threads (4);
     omp_init_lock (& lock);


                                            2

--- PAGE 3 ---
#pragma omp parallel for
    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        omp_set_lock (& lock);
        shared_var += i;
        omp_unset_lock (& lock);
     }

    omp_destroy_lock (& lock);

    printf("shared_var = %d\n", shared_var);
    printf("expected = 10\n");
    return 0;
}

  Run twice. shared var must be 10. If the program hangs, unset is missing.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 4, Lab 2
                            Matrix Multiplication with OpenMP




1 Ideas

• Matrix multiply — C = A × B. Size N = 500. Each C[i][j] is a dot product of row i of A and
  column j of B.

• Every A and B cell is 1, so each C[i][j] equals N = 500. Check C[0][0].

• Three loops: i, j, k. Only the outer i loop is split. Each thread gets different rows of C. No
  reduction. No atomic.

• private(j, k) — each thread has its own j and k. i is already split by parallel for.

• Time with omp get wtime() on both programs. Do not use clock().  Init of A, B, C is outside
   the stopwatch.

                                 C[0][0] must be 500.
                                 speedup = Tserial/Tparallel.


2 Commands

Terminal

 nproc
 nano matrix_serial.c
 gcc -fopenmp matrix_serial.c -o mserial
 ./mserial

 nano matrix_parallel.c
 gcc -fopenmp matrix_parallel.c -o mparallel
 ./mparallel

nproc should be 2 or more, or parallel will not get faster.
nano: Ctrl+O, Enter (save), Ctrl+X (quit).
Forgot ./ →command not found.
Forgot -fopenmp →error on omp.h, or still one thread.
   static on the arrays: 500 × 500 × 3 doubles is too large for the small stack.


3 Serial (one worker)

C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 500

 int main(void) {
     static double A[N][N];
     static double B[N][N];

--- PAGE 2 ---
static double C[N][N];
     int i, j, k;
     double start , end;

     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
             A[i][j] = 1.0;
             B[i][j] = 1.0;
             C[i][j] = 0.0;
          }
      }

     start = omp_get_wtime ();
     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
              for (k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                 C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
               }
          }
      }
     end = omp_get_wtime ();

     printf("C[0][0] = %f (expected %d)\n", C[0][0] , N);
     printf("serial time = %f seconds\n", end - start);
     return 0;
 }

   -fopenmp is only for wtime. There is no #pragma, so this still uses one worker.

4 Parallel (split i only)

The new lines:
C

 omp_set_num_threads (4);

 #pragma omp parallel for private(j, k)

C

 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <omp.h>

 #define N 500

 int main(void) {
     static double A[N][N];
     static double B[N][N];
     static double C[N][N];
     int i, j, k;
     double start , end;

     omp_set_num_threads (4);

     for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
             A[i][j] = 1.0;
             B[i][j] = 1.0;
             C[i][j] = 0.0;
          }
      }


                                            2

--- PAGE 3 ---
start = omp_get_wtime ();
    #pragma omp parallel for private(j, k)
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
         for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
             for (k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
              }
          }
     }
    end = omp_get_wtime ();

    printf("C[0][0] = %f (expected %d)\n", C[0][0] , N);
    printf("parallel time = %f seconds\n", end - start);
    printf("threads = %d\n", omp_get_max_threads ());
    return 0;
}

  C[0][0] must still be 500. Parallel time should be lower than serial if nproc is 2 or more.

                                                         serial time

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 5, Lab 1
                       Distributed computing intro and client–server sockets




1 Ideas

Until the parallel assignment, workers lived inside one process and could share an array (OpenMP /
pthreads). Distributed computing uses separate processes (or machines) that cooperate by sending
messages. There is no shared OpenMP array. This lab stays on one Ubuntu virtual machine.

• Message passing — processes send a copy of bytes (sockets now; MPI later).

• Shared memory — threads of one process share that process’s memory.

• Client–server — one server waits; clients dial. This lab codes that pattern.

• Peer-to-peer (P2P) — equal peers; no single owner (for example BitTorrent).

• Hybrid — a server for control plus peers for heavy traffic (for example BitTorrent with a tracker).

   localhost and port 12345 mean a door on this same machine. The server owns the port. The
client visits it. Start the server first. If the client starts first, the connection is refused.
   encode turns text into bytes for the network. decode turns bytes back into text. That is not
encryption.


2 Commands

Open two terminals. Start the server in the first and leave it running. Start the client in the second.

 nano server.py
 python3 server.py

   Second terminal:

 nano client.py
 python3 client.py


3 Server — server.py


 import socket

 server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET , socket.SOCK_STREAM)
 server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET , socket.SO_REUSEADDR , 1)
 server.bind (("localhost", 12345))
 server.listen (1)
 print("Server listening on port 12345")

 conn , addr = server.accept ()
 print("Connection from", addr)

 data = conn.recv (1024).decode ()
 print("Received:", data)

--- PAGE 2 ---
conn.send("Hello from server!".encode ())
 conn.close ()
 server.close ()


4 Client — client.py


 import socket

 client = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET , socket.SOCK_STREAM)
 client.connect (("localhost", 12345))

 client.send("Hello from client!".encode ())
 response = client.recv (1024).decode ()
 print("Server response:", response)

 client.close ()

   Expected server lines include Received:  Hello from client!. Expected client line: Server
response:  Hello from server!.


5 Check

1. State the difference between message passing and shared memory.

2. Name the three architectures and give one example of each. Which one does this lab code?

3. State what happens when the client starts before the server.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Parallel & Distributed Computing Lab
                                      IMSciences

                            Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan

                              Week 5, Lab 2
                                  Architectures and a Unix pipe




1 Ideas

Last lab coded client–server sockets on localhost.  This lab reviews the three architectures with
examples, then uses a pipe: message passing with no IP and no port.

• Client–server — one server waits; clients dial (web, email apps, Lab 1 sockets).

• Peer-to-peer (P2P) — equal peers swap data. In BitTorrent the file is handled as pieces; a peer
    is a machine in the swarm; a seeder has the complete file and uploads pieces to others. Uploads go
   peer to peer, not to one central movie server.

• Hybrid — a server helps with login or finding peers; heavy traffic still moves among peers (Bit-
   Torrent with a tracker).

  A pipe is a one-way tube. pipe(fd) creates it: fd[1] is the write end, fd[0] is the read end.
fork copies the process into a parent (pid > 0) and a child. In this program the parent writes and
the child reads. Real-world twin: ls | grep.


2 Commands


 nano ipc_pipe.c
 gcc ipc_pipe.c -o ipc
 ./ipc


3 Pipe — ipc pipe.c


 #include <stdio.h>
 #include <unistd.h>
 #include <string.h>

 int main(void) {
     int fd [2];
     pid_t pid;
     char message [] = "Hello from parent";
     char buffer [100];

     pipe(fd);
     pid = fork ();

     if (pid > 0) {
         close(fd [0]);
         write(fd[1], message , strlen(message) + 1);
         close(fd [1]);
      } else {
         close(fd [1]);
         read(fd[0], buffer , sizeof(buffer));

--- PAGE 2 ---
printf("Child received: %s\n", buffer);
         close(fd [0]);
      }

     return 0;
 }

   Expected output:

 Child received: Hello from parent



4 Check

1. Name the three architectures. Give one example each. Which architecture did Lab 1 code?

2. In BitTorrent, state what a piece, a peer, and a seeder are, and where uploads go.

3. In the pipe program, state which end is write, which end is read, and which process writes.

Institute of Management Sciences, Peshawar
SWE 537 — Parallel and Distributed Computing (Lab)
PRACTICE PAPER — Lab Instructor: Saim Sanan
Total marks: 30     Suggested time: 90 minutes
This is a self-made practice paper built from the lab handouts. It is not the real exam and does not contain real exam questions.
Name: | Roll no.: | Section:

Instructions
1. Part A: every question needs a one-line justification. A correct choice with a wrong justification earns 1 mark instead of 2.
2. Parts B and C: scenario questions. Answer each in two lines.
3. Syllabus covered: Week 1 Lab 1 to Week 5 Lab 1. No code is asked on sockets or pipes; only the theory is.
4. Answers are on the last page. Cover it until you finish.
Part A — MCQs and True/False (5 × 2 = 10 marks)
Choose or decide, then justify in one line.
Q1. True or false: SPMD is one of the four classes in Flynn's taxonomy.   [2]
Answer: ______      Justification:

Q2. lscpu shows: CPU(s): 8, Thread(s) per core: 2, Socket(s): 1. What is Core(s) per socket?   [2]
a)  8
b)  4
c)  2
d)  1
Answer: ______      Justification:

Q3. A program has no #pragma. It is compiled with gcc -fopenmp and prints omp_get_max_threads() = 8. How many threads run its for loop?   [2]
a)  8
b)  4
c)  2
d)  1
Answer: ______      Justification:

Q4. True or false: a 20 s program has a 16 s parallelizable loop. Run with 4 workers on the loop, its speedup is 4.   [2]
Answer: ______      Justification:

Q5. Four threads run #pragma omp parallel for on sum += i with no reduction. The printed sum is:   [2]
a)  always equal to the expected value
b)  usually smaller than the expected value
c)  always larger than the expected value
d)  a compile error
Answer: ______      Justification:

Part B — Scenarios: OpenMP constructs (5 × 2 = 10 marks)
Two lines per answer.
Q1. A student writes the program below (N = 100000) and gets a wrong, changing sum. State the problem and the one-line fix.   [2]
#pragma omp parallel
for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    sum += i;
}


Q2. omp_set_num_threads(4) is set. main prints "main before", then a #pragma omp parallel block prints "hello", then main prints "main after". How many times does each line print?   [2]


Q3. A parallel block has #pragma omp sections with four sections A, B, C, D, but only 2 threads. What happens?   [2]


Q4. Inside a parallel block, "single work" prints four times instead of once. What is missing, and how many times does a line placed after the single block print?   [2]


Q5. An "after" line prints before all four "before" lines have printed. Which directive is missing, and what does it do?   [2]


Part C — Scenarios: timing, speedup and distributed computing (5 × 2 = 10 marks)
Two lines per answer.
Q1. A program takes 20 s on one core. 16 s is a loop that can run in parallel; 4 s must stay serial. With 4 workers on the loop, find the parallel time and the speedup. What is the best possible speedup?   [2]


Q2. A student times a 4-thread loop with clock() and the time looks four times too large. Explain why, and name the timer to use.   [2]


Q3. In 500 × 500 matrix multiplication with every A and B cell equal to 1, what must C[0][0] be? Which loop is split across threads, and why is private(j, k) used?   [2]


Q4. Both critical and reduction(+:sum) give the correct total for a sum loop. Which is usually faster, and why?   [2]


Q5. Two programs on one machine exchange bytes by sending messages through a socket; the client starts before the server. (a) How does message passing differ from OpenMP threads? (b) What happens to the client?   [2]



Answer Key — Practice Paper
Each answer is taken from the lab handout named under it. Pass your own justification only if it says the same thing in your words.
Part A
A1. False. Flynn describes the machine (SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD). SPMD is how the code is written: the same C file run by many threads or processes.
Source: Week-1-Lab-2.pdf §1
A2. (b) 4. 1 socket × 4 cores × 2 threads per core = 8 logical processors.
Source: Week-1-Lab-1.pdf §3
A3. (d) 1. With no #pragma the loop is a normal for and uses one thread. omp_get_max_threads() is only how many OpenMP is allowed to hire; -fopenmp only links the timer.
Source: Week-2-Lab-2.pdf §2
A4. False. Time = 4 + 16/4 = 8 s, so speedup = 20/8 = 2.5. The 4 s serial part does not shrink.
Source: Week-2-Lab-1.pdf §2
A5. (b). sum += i is read, add, write; two threads can read the same value and both write back, so the total is usually too small (a race).
Source: Week-3-Lab-1.pdf §1 and §4
Part B
B1. parallel without for makes every thread run the whole loop, and all of them update shared sum, which is a race. Fix: #pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum).
Source: Week-3-Lab-1.pdf §1 and §5; your Lab Week 3 task.c comment
B2. "main before" prints once, "hello" prints four times (once per thread, order can change), "main after" prints once.
Source: Week-3-Lab-1.pdf §3
B3. Each section still runs once. With 2 threads and 4 sections, some threads do two jobs in a row.
Source: Week-3-Lab-2.pdf §1
B4. The #pragma omp single directive is missing. The line after the single block prints once per thread (four times).
Source: Week-3-Lab-2.pdf §4
B5. #pragma omp barrier is missing. Every thread stops at the barrier until all have arrived, then all continue.
Source: Week-4-Lab-1.pdf §1 and §3
Part C
C1. Parallel time = 4 + 16/4 = 8 s. Speedup = 20/8 = 2.5. The loop cannot go below the 4 s serial part, so the best speedup is 20/4 = 5.
Source: Week-2-Lab-1.pdf §2–§5
C2. clock() can add CPU time from every core, so four cores working 1 second can look like 4 seconds. Use omp_get_wtime(), which is wall-clock time.
Source: Week-2-Lab-2.pdf §2
C3. C[0][0] = 500 (each dot product adds N = 500 ones). Only the outer i loop is split, so each thread gets different rows of C. private(j, k) gives each thread its own j and k.
Source: Week-4-Lab-2.pdf §1
C4. reduction is usually faster: each thread sums into a private copy and the copies are added at the end. With critical, threads take turns on sum.
Source: Week-3-Lab-2.pdf §5; Week-4-Lab-1.pdf §1
C5. (a) Message passing sends a copy of bytes between separate processes, with no shared array; OpenMP threads share one process's memory. (b) Start the server first; if the client starts first, the connection is refused.
Source: Week-5-Lab-1.pdf §1 and §5
